questions.stem: The system of state and local laws that enforced racial segregation in the American South was known as:
options: the Great Society
Jim Crow
the Black Codes of 1964
the Freedom Charter
questions.explanation: Jim Crow laws separated Black and white Americans in schools, transport, restaurants and other public places from the late nineteenth century. The Great Society was Lyndon Johnson's reform program of the 1960s.

questions.stem: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) mattered to the civil rights struggle because it:
options: gave African American men the vote in every southern state
made lynching a federal crime punishable by life imprisonment
allowed segregation as long as facilities were 'separate but equal'
struck down racial segregation on interstate buses and in bus stations
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court ruled that segregation was constitutional if facilities were equal, though in practice facilities for Black Americans were usually far worse. The NAACP's legal campaign aimed to overturn this ruling, which it achieved in schooling with Brown in 1954.

questions.stem: Which methods were used in the South before 1965 to stop African Americans from voting?
options: Literacy tests, poll taxes and intimidation
Federal laws that limited voting to landowners
A constitutional ban on Black voters in the South
Compulsory voting in English-only polling booths
questions.explanation: Southern states used literacy tests applied unfairly by white registrars, poll taxes, white primaries and violence or threats of losing work. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) formally banned racial discrimination in voting, so the barriers had to be disguised.

questions.stem: Historians distinguish de jure from de facto segregation. Which is an example of de facto segregation?
options: Mississippi laws forbidding Black and white children from attending the same schools
Virginia laws banning marriage between people of different races
Northern cities where housing and lending practices kept neighbourhoods separate
Alabama laws requiring Black passengers to sit at the back of city buses
questions.explanation: De jure segregation was required by law, as in the southern bus, school and marriage laws. De facto segregation existed in practice without such laws, for example through housing discrimination in northern cities, and proved harder to challenge in the courts.

questions.stem: Which civil rights organisation was founded in 1909 and led the legal campaign against segregation?
options: Southern Christian Leadership Conference
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
Congress of Racial Equality and the Urban League
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People
questions.explanation: The NAACP, founded in 1909, fought segregation mainly through the courts and lobbying. The SCLC was founded in 1957, SNCC in 1960 and CORE in 1942.

questions.stem: How did the ideology of the Nation of Islam differ from that of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference?
options: It favoured integration through the courts rather than through protest
It favoured nonviolent mass protest rather than separation or self-defence
It favoured working within the Democratic Party rather than outside it
It favoured Black separation and self-reliance rather than integration
questions.explanation: The Nation of Islam, whose best-known spokesman was Malcolm X, argued for Black separation, pride and self-reliance and rejected integration. The SCLC, led by Martin Luther King, aimed at integration through nonviolent direct action.

questions.stem: In 1948 President Truman issued Executive Order 9981, which:
options: began desegregating the US armed forces
ended segregation in all public schools
banned poll taxes in federal elections
created the Civil Rights Commission
questions.explanation: Executive Order 9981 required equal treatment in the armed forces, leading to their desegregation over the following years. Poll taxes in federal elections were banned by the Twenty-fourth Amendment in 1964, and the Civil Rights Commission was set up by the 1957 Civil Rights Act.

questions.stem: Which organisation was founded in 1957 with Martin Luther King as its president?
options: National Association of Colored Women
Montgomery Improvement Association
Southern Christian Leadership Conference
Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
questions.explanation: King and other Black church leaders founded the SCLC in 1957 to coordinate nonviolent protest across the South. The Montgomery Improvement Association, which King also led, had been formed in 1955 to run the bus boycott, and SNCC was formed by students in 1960.

questions.stem: Who was the NAACP's chief lawyer in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka?
options: Thurgood Marshall
Earl Warren
Medgar Evers
Bayard Rustin
questions.explanation: Thurgood Marshall led the NAACP Legal Defense Fund's case and later became the first African American Supreme Court justice in 1967. Earl Warren was the Chief Justice who wrote the court's decision.

questions.stem: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled that:
options: private schools must admit students of every race or lose their tax exemption
segregated public schools were unconstitutional, being inherently unequal
segregated schools were legal provided Black schools received the same funding
states must bus children between districts to achieve racial balance in schools
questions.explanation: The unanimous decision held that separate schools were 'inherently unequal', overturning Plessy in public education. It did not order busing, which came later, and a second ruling in 1955 called for desegregation only 'with all deliberate speed', which the South exploited to delay.

questions.stem: Why did the Brown decision of 1954 lead to so little school desegregation in the Deep South over the next decade?
options: African American parents preferred to keep their children in separate schools
The court set no deadline, and southern states organised 'massive resistance'
The court reversed the decision in 1955 after protests from southern governors
Congress passed a law suspending the decision until all states had agreed
questions.explanation: Brown II (1955) required desegregation 'with all deliberate speed' but set no timetable, and southern politicians responded with massive resistance, including the 1956 Southern Manifesto and school closures. The decision was never reversed or suspended.

questions.stem: The Montgomery Bus Boycott began in December 1955 after Rosa Parks:
options: was turned away from voting at the Montgomery county courthouse
was barred from enrolling at the University of Alabama
was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger
was refused service at a whites-only lunch counter in a downtown city store
questions.explanation: Parks, secretary of the Montgomery NAACP branch, was arrested on 1 December 1955. Her arrest sparked a boycott organised by the Montgomery Improvement Association, which chose the young minister Martin Luther King as its president.

questions.stem: How did the Montgomery Bus Boycott end in December 1956?
options: The bus company went bankrupt and the city took over the service
Alabama's governor ordered the city buses desegregated to end the protest
Congress passed a law banning segregation on all public transport
The Supreme Court upheld a ruling that bus segregation was unconstitutional
questions.explanation: In Browder v. Gayle a federal court ruled Montgomery's bus segregation unconstitutional, and the Supreme Court upheld the ruling in November 1956. The boycott ended when the order took effect in December, after about 381 days. It showed the power of combining mass action with legal challenges.

questions.stem: In September 1957 President Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne Division to Little Rock, Arkansas, to:
options: enforce the result of a contested local election
protect nine Black students enrolling at Central High School
arrest Governor Orval Faubus for defying the Supreme Court
end a riot that followed a bus boycott in the city
questions.explanation: Governor Orval Faubus used the Arkansas National Guard to keep the Little Rock Nine out of Central High School. When a hostile crowd gathered, Eisenhower sent federal troops to protect the students, the first use of federal troops in the South for this purpose since Reconstruction.

questions.stem: The sit-in movement of 1960 began when four Black college students:
options: refused to leave a whites-only bus station waiting room in Montgomery, Alabama
occupied the office of the governor of Mississippi in Jackson
marched from Selma to Montgomery to demand the right to vote
sat at a whites-only Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina
questions.explanation: On 1 February 1960 four students from North Carolina A&T sat at the Greensboro Woolworth counter and asked to be served. Sit-ins spread rapidly across the South, and many lunch counters were desegregated within months.

questions.stem: The Freedom Rides of 1961 were organised to test:
options: whether rulings against segregation in interstate travel were obeyed
whether southern states would allow African Americans to register to vote
whether northern cities would desegregate their public housing projects
whether federal troops would protect students entering southern universities
questions.explanation: CORE sent integrated groups on buses through the South to test Boynton v. Virginia (1960), which banned segregation in interstate bus terminals. Riders were attacked in Alabama, and a bus was set on fire near Anniston. The Interstate Commerce Commission then ordered terminals desegregated.

questions.stem: The Birmingham campaign of 1963 is seen as a turning point mainly because:
options: the city's police commissioner, Bull Connor, resigned and joined the civil rights movement
it was the first campaign in which Martin Luther King was arrested and imprisoned
it ended with Alabama passing its own civil rights law before the federal one
television images of police dogs and fire hoses used on young protesters shocked the nation
questions.explanation: Images of Bull Connor's police turning dogs and fire hoses on marchers, many of them children, drew national and international outrage. Kennedy announced a civil rights bill soon afterwards. King had been arrested before, in Montgomery and Albany, and Connor did not change sides.

questions.stem: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom of 28 August 1963 is significant because it:
options: was the first civil rights protest that was supported by the Ku Klux Klan
led President Kennedy to send federal troops to occupy the state of Alabama
built pressure for a civil rights bill and featured King's best-known speech
forced Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act on the very same afternoon
questions.explanation: Around 250,000 people gathered peacefully at the Lincoln Memorial, showing mass support for civil rights legislation. The Civil Rights Act followed in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965.

questions.stem: The White Citizens' Councils, first formed in Mississippi in 1954, opposed desegregation mainly by:
options: taking legal action in the Supreme Court to overturn the Brown decision itself
standing their own candidates in national elections across the North
organising armed militias to fight federal troops in Little Rock
economic pressure such as sacking workers and denying loans to activists
questions.explanation: Unlike the Klan, the Councils were respectable middle-class groups of businessmen and politicians. They punished civil rights supporters economically, through dismissals, evictions and loan refusals. They did not field national candidates or fight federal troops.

questions.stem: In September 1963 a bomb at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama:
options: was planted by federal agents to discredit the civil rights movement
destroyed Martin Luther King's home during the Montgomery boycott
killed four African American girls and was the work of Klan members
killed Medgar Evers, the NAACP field secretary in Mississippi
questions.explanation: Ku Klux Klan members bombed the church on 15 September 1963, killing four girls and causing national outrage. Medgar Evers was shot outside his home in Jackson, Mississippi, in June 1963. King's home was bombed during the Montgomery boycott, but no one was killed.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the Ku Klux Klan and the White Citizens' Councils as opponents of civil rights?
options: The Klan worked mainly through state legislatures, while the Councils carried out bombings
Both relied mainly on Supreme Court cases to defend segregation in the South
Both were founded in direct response to the Voting Rights Act of 1965
The Klan relied on terror and violence, while the Councils used economic and political pressure
questions.explanation: The Klan used bombings, beatings and murders, while the Councils presented themselves as law-abiding and used dismissals, boycotts and political influence. Both were active well before 1965; the Councils formed in response to Brown in 1954.

questions.stem: On 7 March 1965, 'Bloody Sunday', Alabama state troopers attacked voting-rights marchers at:
options: the Lincoln Memorial in Washington
Central High School in Little Rock
the Lorraine Motel in Memphis
the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma
questions.explanation: Marchers setting out from Selma for Montgomery were beaten and tear-gassed by state troopers as they crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Television coverage shocked the nation and helped push the Voting Rights Act through Congress. King was assassinated at the Lorraine Motel in 1968.

questions.stem: Which events most directly led to the Voting Rights Act of 1965?
options: The assassination of Malcolm X and the founding of the Black Panthers
Violence against marchers at Selma and the murders of voting-rights activists
The riots in Watts and Detroit and the published report of the Kerner Commission
The Montgomery Bus Boycott and the Brown v. Board of Education ruling
questions.explanation: The murders of three Freedom Summer workers in Mississippi in 1964 and the attack by Alabama state troopers on marchers at Selma's Edmund Pettus Bridge on 7 March 1965 ('Bloody Sunday') created national pressure. President Johnson signed the Act in August 1965. Detroit and the Kerner Commission came later.

questions.stem: What did the Voting Rights Act of 1965 do?
options: Suspended literacy tests and allowed federal examiners to register voters
Gave the vote to all citizens aged 18 and over in federal elections
Required every state to hold elections on the same day each year
Banned racial segregation in hotels, restaurants and all other public places
questions.explanation: The Act suspended literacy tests in areas with low registration and sent federal examiners to register voters, and Black registration in the South rose sharply. Banning segregation in public accommodations was the Civil Rights Act of 1964; the vote at 18 came in 1971.

questions.stem: Freedom Summer (1964) brought northern student volunteers to Mississippi. Which aim best explains why organisers recruited mainly white volunteers?
options: They believed white students would be better at teaching literacy than local Black activists
They had been ordered by President Johnson to include white students in all of their civil rights work
They wanted to avoid any contact with local African American churches and organisations
They expected violence against white students to draw national attention and federal protection
questions.explanation: Organisers in SNCC and CORE knew that violence against Black Mississippians was largely ignored, and expected that attention to white volunteers would bring the media and federal government. The disappearance and murder of three workers, two of them white, did bring national attention.

questions.stem: The riots in Newark and Detroit in the summer of 1967 drew attention to:
options: the exclusion of Black voters from the southern Democratic primaries
segregation on interstate buses and in railway stations
poverty, unemployment and police conduct in northern city ghettos
the refusal of southern states to obey the Brown decision
questions.explanation: The riots showed that legal equality in the South had not solved poverty, poor housing, unemployment and police conduct in northern cities. President Johnson set up the Kerner Commission, which blamed white racism and urban conditions.

questions.stem: What followed the assassination of Martin Luther King in Memphis on 4 April 1968?
options: Riots in more than 100 cities and the passing of the Fair Housing Act
The immediate passing of the Voting Rights Act and the end of all riots
The election of Malcolm X as leader of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference
A Supreme Court ruling that ended segregation in all public schools
questions.explanation: Unrest broke out in more than 100 cities, and Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1968, known as the Fair Housing Act, within a week. The Voting Rights Act dated from 1965, and Malcolm X had been killed in 1965.

questions.stem: Malcolm X rose to prominence in the late 1950s and early 1960s as a spokesman for:
options: the Nation of Islam
the NAACP
the SCLC
the National Urban League
questions.explanation: Malcolm X was the Nation of Islam's best-known minister until he left it in 1964. He then founded his own organisations and moderated some views before he was assassinated in February 1965.

questions.stem: In 1966 SNCC chairman Stokely Carmichael popularised the slogan 'Black Power'. This reflected:
options: a demand that white volunteers lead the movement in the South
frustration with nonviolence and a call for Black pride and self-determination
a decision to merge SNCC with the NAACP and to focus on cases in the courts
support for President Johnson's decision to send many more troops to Vietnam
questions.explanation: Many young activists had lost faith in nonviolence and white liberal allies after years of violence. Black Power stressed pride, community control and self-defence, and SNCC soon excluded white members. SNCC opposed the Vietnam War.

questions.stem: The Black Panther Party, founded in Oakland, California, in 1966 by Huey Newton and Bobby Seale, was known for:
options: a strategy of strict nonviolence based closely on Christian teaching and Gandhi
leading the legal challenge in Brown v. Board of Education
armed patrols to monitor police, and community programs such as free breakfasts
organising lunch counter sit-ins across North Carolina and Tennessee in 1960
questions.explanation: The Panthers carried guns openly to watch police in Black neighbourhoods and ran community programs, including free breakfasts for children. The FBI targeted them heavily through its COINTELPRO program.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the influence of Malcolm X on the movement to 1972?
options: His stress on pride and self-defence shaped Black Power after his death
His leadership of the SCLC ended King's policy of nonviolent mass protest
His support for integration won over white liberals in the North
His campaign of court cases ended segregation in southern schools
questions.explanation: Malcolm X's message of Black pride, self-reliance and self-defence inspired Carmichael, the Black Panthers and the wider Black Power movement. He never led the SCLC and rejected integration for most of his career.

questions.stem: Ella Baker is significant in the civil rights movement mainly because she:
options: refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery before Rosa Parks
helped found SNCC and promoted grassroots, group-centred leadership
was the first African American woman elected to the US Senate
led the NAACP's legal team in the Brown v. Board of Education case itself
questions.explanation: Baker worked for the NAACP and the SCLC and organised the 1960 conference at Shaw University that created SNCC. She encouraged young activists to stay independent and to develop local leaders rather than rely on a single charismatic figure.

questions.stem: Fannie Lou Hamer became nationally known in 1964 when she:
options: led the sit-in at the Woolworth lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina
argued the case for desegregating buses before the US Supreme Court
challenged the all-white Mississippi delegation at the Democratic convention
became the first Black student to enrol at the University of Mississippi
questions.explanation: Hamer, a sharecropper who had been evicted for registering to vote, spoke for the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party at the 1964 convention, describing the violence faced by voters. James Meredith was the first Black student at the University of Mississippi in 1962.

questions.stem: Martin Luther King's leadership of the movement was based above all on:
options: Black separatism and self-reliance
legal action in the courts alone
nonviolent direct action
armed community self-defence
questions.explanation: King drew on Christian teaching and Gandhi's methods to lead nonviolent protests designed to expose injustice and win public sympathy. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the limits of Martin Luther King's influence in his final years?
options: His 1966 Chicago campaign against housing segregation won little
The Montgomery boycott of 1955-56 made him a national figure
His Nobel Peace Prize of 1964 brought him international recognition
The 1963 March on Washington drew a crowd of about 250,000 people
questions.explanation: King's 1966 campaign in Chicago met violent white resistance and won only limited promises on housing, showing that his methods worked less well against de facto segregation in the North. He also faced challenges from Black Power advocates. The other events show his growing influence.

questions.stem: In 1962 President Kennedy sent federal marshals and troops to the University of Mississippi to enforce the enrolment of:
options: Huey Newton
James Meredith
Medgar Evers
Stokely Carmichael
questions.explanation: James Meredith, an air force veteran, won a court order to enrol at the all-white university. Riots broke out on the campus, and Kennedy sent marshals and troops to restore order and see him enrolled. Medgar Evers was the NAACP's Mississippi field secretary.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes President Kennedy's record on civil rights?
options: He ended segregation in the armed forces by executive order in 1961
Cautious at first, he proposed a major civil rights bill in June 1963
He passed the Civil Rights Act soon after taking office in early 1961
He opposed all federal action and refused to protect the Freedom Riders
questions.explanation: Kennedy at first avoided civil rights legislation to keep southern Democrats on side, though he sent marshals to protect Freedom Riders and James Meredith. After Birmingham he went on television in June 1963 and proposed a civil rights bill, which passed under Johnson in 1964. The armed forces were desegregated under Truman.

questions.stem: Which law, signed by President Johnson, banned segregation in public places such as hotels and restaurants and discrimination in employment?
options: Voting Rights Act of 1965
Fair Housing Act of 1968
Civil Rights Act of 1964
Civil Rights Act of 1957
questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed segregation in public accommodations and discrimination in employment, creating the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. The 1957 Act, under Eisenhower, dealt mainly with voting and set up the Civil Rights Commission.

questions.stem: A historian argues that federal governments followed rather than led the civil rights movement. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Johnson used his skills in Congress to overcome a long filibuster by southern senators in 1964
Major civil rights laws came after protests such as Birmingham and Selma had drawn national attention
Truman's 1948 executive order desegregated the armed forces before any mass protest movement had begun
Eisenhower appointed Earl Warren, who then wrote the unanimous Brown decision in 1954
questions.explanation: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 followed Birmingham and the March on Washington, and the Voting Rights Act followed Selma, suggesting governments acted under pressure from activists. Truman's order shows federal action ahead of mass protest, and Johnson's skill shows federal leadership, so both weaken the argument.

questions.stem: Which statement best assesses the extent of change for African Americans by 1972?
options: Little had changed, because the Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act were never enforced
Segregation had ended in the North, but southern states had won the right to keep it by law
Legal segregation and voting barriers had largely gone, but poverty and de facto segregation remained
Full economic equality had been achieved, but segregation laws still remained in most southern states
questions.explanation: By 1972 de jure segregation had been dismantled and Black voter registration and the number of Black elected officials had risen greatly, especially in the South. But economic inequality, poor housing and de facto segregation in schools and neighbourhoods persisted, as the 1967 riots and the busing disputes showed.
